title: The Keys of Hollowmere
subtitle: The Legend of Ser Aldric
teaser: The grand master of the Order of Bronze sold the wolves the keys to the town his knights had sworn to guard. He forgot to ask the youngest of them.

sections.heading: I. The Oath on the Bridge
paragraphs: Aldric was eighteen when he knelt on the bridge of Hollowmere at dawn, raised his sword to the sky, and waited for the light.
It didn’t come. It never did.

Four hundred years before, Saint Edda had held that bridge against the first wolves out of the north, and when she knelt on it to swear she would guard it forever, the sun broke through the clouds and struck her blade. Every knight of Bronze since had sworn her oath on that spot at dawn. The chaplains said the light would come to any knight who truly meant it. Nobody living had seen it.
“Between the water and the wolves,” Aldric said. “Till the wolves are gone, or the water dries, or I fall. By oath, I stand.”
The clouds stayed shut. A gull complained. Grand Master Gerrold Crane laid a gloved hand on his shoulder and lifted him to his feet.
“Don’t look so stricken,” Crane said kindly. “It didn’t come for me either.”

Crane was the finest speaker on the lake: tall, silver-haired, with a voice like warm oil. At his belt hung the keys of Hollowmere, three bronze keys as long as a man’s forearm. Only the grand master carried them.

Hollowmere sat on an island in a cold lake, joined to the northern shore by that one long bridge. Ninety knights lived in the chapter house on the hill and took a tithe of every catch and harvest. Their bronze had gone green at the joints. The masters held fat lands on the shore, granted long ago for courage, and somewhere along the way the courage had stayed in the songs and the lands had stayed in the families.
Aldric didn’t care. He scrubbed his bronze till it shone, took the gatehouse night watch nobody else wanted, and thought there was nothing finer in the world than a knight of Bronze.
He went on thinking so for almost a year.

sections.heading: II. The Price of Keys
paragraphs: The Wolf King came out of the north in the spring, with ten thousand spears.
He had won his title the northern way, by killing the last king and taking his pelt. Among the wolves the pelt was the crown, and the spears went where the pelt told them.

The pelt told them to go to Hollowmere. Within a week the northern shore was black with tents, and a herald bellowed terms across the water. Open the gate, and the town would live. Shut it, and the wolves would build a ramp of bodies to the top.
The masters met that night in the chapter hall with the doors shut. Aldric was on guard outside them, which is how he heard every word.

Crane spoke for an hour, and he spoke well. Ninety knights against ten thousand spears was not courage, he said. It was arithmetic, and the answer was ninety dead knights and a town burned anyway. The Wolf King did not want Hollowmere’s blood, only its fish and its tithe. Better that a reasonable man collect that tithe than a wolf.
“He has offered terms,” Crane said. “Our lives, and our lands on the northern shore, held from him. In return, the gate opens at dawn.”
“And the town?” someone asked.
“Towns survive a change of masters. I have read a great deal of history.”
They voted. It wasn’t close. Before midnight Crane’s secretary rowed across to the wolves with the keys of Hollowmere wrapped in a cloth, and came back with the cloth.
Aldric went to the gatehouse.

He dropped the portcullis and cut through the winch chain so no one could raise it again. He barred the inner door with every beam in the guardroom. Then he climbed onto the roof and shouted into the dark streets that the masters had sold the gate, the wolves were coming at dawn, and the gate would hold as long as he did.
“So go,” he told them. “All of you. Go now.”

sections.heading: III. A Day and a Night
paragraphs: The wolves crossed the bridge at first light, turned the bronze keys in the great gate, swung it open, and found the portcullis down behind it and a young knight looking at them through the bars.
Then they tried to get in.

Saint Edda had built that gatehouse for exactly this, and it remembered how. Aldric poured boiling lamp oil through the murder holes. He dropped the guardroom’s millstones on the ram. When they brought ladders to the towers, he met each one at the top with his greatsword and sent it back down full. He did not sit down once.

Behind him, Hollowmere was taking itself apart. Fishing boats towed strings of rafts made from doors, tables, bedframes and chapel pews. The wolves had no boats, and two thousand people went out across the cold lake to the southern shore. Every time Aldric looked back from the roof there were fewer chimneys smoking and more rafts on the water.

The knights of Bronze watched from the chapter house windows. They could have broken his door down, but the town was watching too, and not even Crane wanted to be seen dragging the last man off the gate.
So near midnight, he came to talk.

“Aldric,” said the warm voice through the oak. “You have made your point, and made it well. The town is leaving. Now stand down. The King admires courage. Come out, keep your sword, and I will make you a master by midsummer.”
Aldric leaned his forehead on the door. He was so tired he could hear his own heart.
“What did you swear, Grand Master? On the bridge?”
There was a long silence.
“Words, Aldric. Pretty, old words.”
“Then I’ll say them for both of us.”

And he said Saint Edda’s oath through the door while the wolves hammered at the portcullis below. “Between the water and the wolves. Till the wolves are gone, or the water dries, or I fall. By oath, I stand.”
Crane didn’t answer. His footsteps went away down the stairs, and Aldric went back to work.

sections.heading: IV. The Bridge at Dawn
paragraphs: By the second dawn the last raft had crossed the lake. Aldric’s oil was gone, the portcullis was bent like a fork, and the wolves had stopped attacking, because their king had come down to the gate himself.

He stood a head taller than any of his men, the gray pelt over his shoulders and the wolf’s head for a hood, leaning on an axe with a blade like a half moon. On a thong at his belt hung the keys of Hollowmere.
“Your town is gone,” he called up. “Your masters are mine. Come down and fight me on the bridge. Win, and my army goes home. Lose, and I hang you from your own gate.”
Aldric came down.

He walked out onto the bridge, raised his sword before his face, and lowered its point to the stones at the Wolf King’s feet. It was the salute of the Order of Bronze. It meant: I see you, and here I stand.
The Wolf King laughed at it. Then he came.

He was faster than any man that size had a right to be, and Aldric had been fighting for a day and a night. The first blow split his shield. The second laid open his ribs. The third drove him down onto one knee, on the exact stone where he had sworn. The Wolf King lifted the axe in both hands.
Over the far hills, the sun came up. Aldric raised his sword.
The light came down on it.

Not slanting dawn light. It fell straight out of the sky like a pillar, onto the blade and nothing else, so bright that the lake went white and ten thousand men on the northern shore flung their arms over their eyes. The Wolf King, standing right in front of it, saw nothing at all.
Aldric came up off his knee and put the sword through him.

He unpinned the gray pelt from the body and put it on his own shoulders, where it sat heavy and stank of smoke. Then he walked to the far end of the bridge and faced ten thousand spears, wearing their crown.
“Go home,” he said.
They went home.
By then the knights of Bronze were riding down from the hill in their green armor, the grand master at their head, and the first rafts were coming back across the lake.
“Ser Aldric!” Crane cried, loud enough to carry over the water. “The Order salutes you!”
Aldric bent over the dead king, cut the keys from his belt, and held them up to the grand master’s saddle.
“Grand Master,” he said, just as loudly. “You dropped these.”
Out on the lake, two thousand people stopped rowing.

sections.heading: V. The Shield of Hollowmere
paragraphs: The Order cast him out a week later, in the chapter hall, with the doors shut. The charge was disobedience to his grand master in time of war. Crane read it beautifully. Then he held out his hand, and Aldric laid his sword in it.
“You made us look like cowards,” Crane said quietly.
“No, Grand Master,” said Aldric. “I only stood next to you.”

They say that one morning, before anyone else was awake, Crane carried that sword out onto the bridge and raised it to the dawn, and stood there a long time with his arm shaking. It didn’t come for him either.

The town gave its own verdict. The fishermen stopped paying the tithe, and the council walked up the hill with half of Hollowmere behind it and took back the keys and the Order’s lands. The smiths melted them down, beat the bronze into a round shield, struck it with the town’s whirlpool seal, and gave it to the man the Order had thrown out. A town that had been sold once would rather keep a man than a key.
The Order of Bronze lasted nine more years. Gerrold Crane died grand master of eleven old men in a cold house, with an empty ring on his belt where the keys used to hang.
Aldric carries a plain greatsword now, made by the smiths of Hollowmere, and the light comes down on it anyway. It was never in the sword.

He still wears the Order’s crested helm, and the Wolf King’s pelt across his shoulders. By the law of the north that makes him their king, and somewhere past the mountains ten thousand spears are waiting for the man in the pelt to call them. He never has. He wears it so they remember who sent them home.

He fights in the duelling rings now, and he will tell you why. The Order of Bronze was sold in a shut room at night, by men who never had to look at the people they sold. A ring is the opposite of that room. Everyone watches. Nothing in it can be settled with a key. Lords’ men still come to his tent with purses, asking him to go down in the third round. He salutes them, and they have learned what that means.

Before every bout he gives his opponent the salute of an Order that no longer exists, because it is older than the men who broke it. Then he raises his blade. At eighteen he knelt on a bridge and waited for the light. He doesn’t wait anymore. He says the last four words of the oath, and it comes.
